The present complaint is filed under section 2(d) read with section 200 of code of criminal procedure against the accused seeking to punish him for the offence punishable under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act ( in short referred as "N.I. Act").

02. The thumbnail of the averments of the complaint are as under;
It is averred in the complaint that, the complainant, accused and his father by name Srinivas are well known to each other and are were closely associated.
On the eve of this relationship, on 13.11.2011, the complainant has advanced a sum of Rs.1,50,000/- to the accused by way of cheque bearing No.16858800 drawn on Andhra Bank, Bannerghatta Road Branch.
Thereafter, in the month of December 2017, the accused again has requested the complainant to advance him a sum of Rs.5,00,000/-.

Accordingly, in order to keep the friendship and also trust, the complainant had pledged his family gold ornament with Andra Bank and took loan and paid a sum of Rs. 4,50,000/-
on 12.12.2017 by way of cash.
In all the accused has borrowed Rs.6,00,000/- from the complainant.

Thereafter, due to ill health of the uncle of the complainant, when he had requested the accused for the repayment of the Rs.6,00,000/-, but the accused has failed to pay the same, the accused has issued a cheque bearing No.444621 Dated 18.01.2018 for Rs.6,00,000/- drawn on Andra Bank,
Bengaluru Branch, Bengaluru thereafter in favour of the complainant for the discharge of liability of the complainant.
When the complainant has presented the above said cheque for encashment through his banker for encashment, it has returned unpaid due to 'Account Closed' as per banker's memo dated on 05.07.2017.
Thereafter, the complainant got issued demand notice on 05.02.2018 to the accused and the said notice was duly served to the accused on 07.02.2018.
Inspite of service of demand notice, accused neither has paid the cheque amount not has given any reply.
Thus, the cause of action for the complaint arose on 03.03.2018.
Accordingly, this complaint is filed within time and has sought to convict the accused by granting compensation under section 357 of Code of Criminal Procedure double of the cheque amount.

03. On presentation of the complaint and after verification of the averments of the complaint as well as the annexed documents, this court took the cognizance for the offence punishable under section 138 of NI Act.

As per the verdicts of the Hon'ble Apex court in the case of Indian Bank Association and others V/s Union of India and others, the sworn statement of the complainant has been recorded by way of examination-in-chief as PW.1 and got marked in all seven documents at Ex.P.01 to Ex.P.07.

15. Section 118(a) is the special presumption, it contemplates that, " once the cheque has been drawn from an account by mentioning some consideration amount, it shall be presumed that, the said cheque was issued for some consideration and it has been accepted untill the contrary is proved.

Section 139 of NI Act provides another important legal presumptions which favours the holder of the cheque stating that, the holder of cheque has received the cheque of the nature referred to another section 138 of the discharge in whole or in part of any debt or other liability unless the contrary is proved.

The Learned Defense Counsel vehemently argued that, when the financial capacity of the complainant is disputed, the initial burden is on the complainant to prove his case beyond all reasonable doubts, then only the legal presumptions under sections 118 and 139 of NI Act shall go in favour of the complainant.

In support of his contention, the Learned Defense Counsel has relied following verdicts of the Hon'ble Apex Court i.e.,
01. AIR 2019 SC 1983 Basalingappa Vs. Mudibasappa 02. 2019(16) SCC 83 Sri.Daneshwari Traders Vs. Sanjay Jain and another.

sentences.text: Wherein the larger bench of the Hon'ble Apex Court have clearly held that, ' once the signature on the cheque is admitted and also the issuance of the cheque from the account of the accused is admitted, the presumption under section 118(a) & 139 of NI Act, shall operate in favour of the complainant and the obligation shifts upon the accused to discharge the presumption imposed upon him.
Therefore, with due respect of the ratio laid down in the relied judgments by the Learned Defense Counsel, they are not applicable to the case on hand.

Further,
even in the recent verdict, the Hon'ble Apex Court, in the case of Rajesh Jain Vs. Ajay Singh, the ratio is laid down.

Thus, from the verdicts of the larger bench of the Hon'ble Apex Court and the recent verdict of the Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Rajesh Jain Vs. Ajay Singh, now it has became well settled law that, 'once the issuance of cheque and signature thereon has been admitted,
then the legal presumptions under section 118 and 139 of NI Act shall operates against the accused and works in favour of the complainant.

The burden shifts on the accused to rebut the statutory presumption under section 118(a) & 139 of NI Act by raising probable defense and also proving the said probable defense by producing evidence on preponderance of probabilities.
Once, the accused establishes and proved his defense and thereby rebuts the legal presumptions, the onus shifts on the complainant to establish and prove his beyond all reasonable doubts.

Therefore, the above contrary contention of the Learned Defense Counsel in respect of well established proposition of law in the above relied judgments is not tenable and such a contention is turned down.

In another recent and leading judgment of the Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Tedhi Singh Vs. Narayan Das Mahant, in Crl.Appeal No.362/2022 also reported in 2022 Live Law (SC) 275, it has been held that;
' If the accused put forth his defense in the beginning itself by giving reply and has disputed the financial capacity of the complainant, then only the burden shifts on the complainant to prove his financial capacity beyond all reasonable doubts and only there upon, the legal presumptions under section 118 and 139 of NI Act shall operates in favour of the complainant.'

Thus, the burden do not shifts on the complainant to prove his financial capacity.

The burden shifts on the accused to rebut the statutory presumption under section 118(a) & 139 of NI Act.

The Learned Defense Counsel himself has relied the verdict of Hon'ble Apex Court reported in 2019(5) SCC 418, in the case of Basalingappa Vs. Mudibasappa, wherein the ratio of law is laid down as to how the legal presumption shall be drawn, how the said presumptions can be rebutted and what is the standard of evidence to prove the probable defense by the accused and also what is the standard of evidence required by the complainant to prove his case beyond all reasonable doubts .
Further, it has been held that, while proving his probable defense, the accused may rely upon the evidence of complainant or he may produce his own evidence.

Here, in the case on hand, the Learned Defense Counsel has conducted a marathon cross examination of PW.1 and also the oral evidence of accused has been adduced as DW.1 so also adduced the evidence of father of accused as DW.2 and also produced in all twenty five documents at Ex.D.1 to Ex.D.25 before the court and also to corroborate the oral evidence of DW.1 & DW.2.
There is no bar to the accused to put forth his defense at any time during the enquiry or trial, when he fails to put forth his defense by giving reply notice in NI Act provision.

Let me discuss firstly the evidence elicited during the cross examination of PW.1 and to find out whether the accused has put forth his defense and also has elicited any material evidence from the mouth of PW.1 to prove his defense.

the father of the accused has put chit amount of Rs.10,20,000/- with him in the year 2015- 2016 and in the month of May 2016, since the father of the accused was in need of money.

For the said suggestion, PW.1 has answered partly, stating that, he could not remember in respect of the suggestion that, the father of accused had became the member of chit amount of Rs.10,20,000/- in the year 2015-2016 and he was in need of money in the year 2016.

opennyai_summary.facts:
The present complaint is filed under section 2(d) read with section 200 of code of criminal procedure against the accused seeking to punish him for the offence punishable under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act ( in short referred as "N.I. Act").
Thus, the cause of action for the complaint arose on 03.03.2018.
Accordingly, this complaint is filed within time and has sought to convict the accused by granting compensation under section 357 of Code of Criminal Procedure double of the cheque amount.
03. On presentation of the complaint and after verification of the averments of the complaint as well as the annexed documents, this court took the cognizance for the offence punishable under section 138 of NI Act.
As per the verdicts of the Hon'ble Apex court in the case of Indian Bank Association and others V/s Union of India and others, the sworn statement of the complainant has been recorded by way of examination-in-chief as PW.1 and got marked in all seven documents at Ex.P.01 to Ex.P.07.
The substance of accusation has been recorded and read over to the accused,
he pleaded not guilty.
On filing application by the complainant under section 145(1) of NI Act, sworn statement of the complainant has been treated as examination in chief.
Similarly, on filing application under section 145(2) of NI Act, the accused has been permitted to cross examine PW.1.
On completion of the trial of the complainant's side, the statement of accused under section 313 of Code of Criminal Procedure has been recorded and read over to the accused, the incriminating material found in the trial of the case of the complainant.
Wherein, the Hon'ble Apex Court pleased to held that, ' in order to drawn the presumption under section 118(a) & 139 of NI Act, the burden was on the complainant to show that,
he had sufficient funds for having advanced the money to the accused.
Further held that, the burden on the complainant to establish foundational facts to raise presumption under 139 of NI Act.
opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
To substantiate and establish this fact before the court beyond reasonable doubts as per the verdict of the Hon'ble Apex court in the case of Indian Bank Association and others V/s Union of India and others , the sworn statement of the complainant has been treated as affidavit evidence.
The oral evidence and documents are contrary to the averments of the complainant.
Section 118 and 139 of NI Act do not favours the complainant as such, the Income Tax returns of PW.1 not produced.
However, in the judgment reported in 2010(11) SCC 441 in case of Rangappa Vs. Mohan, in another judgment reported in 2021(5)SCC 283 in the case of Kalamani Tex and another Vs.
P.Balasubramaniyan and in another judgment reported in 2022(1) SCC 742 in the case of Trayambak S.Hegde Vs. Sripad.
Wherein the larger bench of the Hon'ble Apex Court have clearly held that, ' once the signature on the cheque is admitted and also the issuance of the cheque from the account of the accused is admitted, the presumption under section 118(a) & 139 of NI Act, shall operate in favour of the complainant and the obligation shifts upon the accused to discharge the presumption imposed upon him.
Therefore, with due respect of the ratio laid down in the relied judgments by the Learned Defense Counsel, they are not applicable to the case on hand.
Thus, from the verdicts of the larger bench of the Hon'ble Apex Court and the recent verdict of the Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Rajesh Jain Vs. Ajay Singh, now it has became well settled law that, 'once the issuance of cheque and signature thereon has been admitted,
then the legal presumptions under section 118 and 139 of NI Act shall operates against the accused and works in favour of the complainant.
In another recent and leading judgment of the Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Tedhi Singh Vs. Narayan Das Mahant, in Crl.Appeal No.362/2022 also reported in 2022 Live Law (SC) 275, it has been held that;
' If the accused put forth his defense in the beginning itself by giving reply and has disputed the financial capacity of the complainant, then only the burden shifts on the complainant to prove his financial capacity beyond all reasonable doubts and only there upon, the legal presumptions under section 118 and 139 of NI Act shall operates in favour of the complainant.'
Here, in the case on hand,
admittedly even after receipt of demand notice personally by the accused, he has not sent his reply notice.
Therefore, no such defense has been taken by the accused with regard to financial capacity of the complainant in the beginning itself by giving his reply.
Thus, the burden do not shifts on the complainant to prove his financial capacity.
17. On meticulous scrutiny of evidence of DW.1 and DW.2, they have clearly stated that, the complainant had taken two signed blank cheques of present accused and two blank cheques of DW.2 as a security in a chit transaction.
Therefore, by considering these material evidence, it clearly appears that, the accused is admitting the issuance of cheque at Ex.P.1 for some consideration towards the discharge of legally enforceable debt or liability of the complainant, therefore the statutory presumptions under section 118(a) & 139 of NI Act shall goes in favour of the complainant and operates against the accused.
The burden shifts on the accused to rebut the statutory presumption under section 118(a) & 139 of NI Act.
Further, present complaint has filed MC cases against his wife by name Yashoda Bai and similarly the wife of present complainant also filed petition against the present complainant under Domestic Violence Act.
In a criminal case the character of the accused is irrelevant for consideration as a evidence, but the character of the complainant can be taken into consideration in deciding the trust worthy and truthfulness of the case of the complainant.
Thus, by the oral evidence of DW.1 & DW.2 coupled with the documentary evidences placed on record under Ex.D.1 to Ex.D.25 and the material evidence culled out during the cross examination of DW.1, I am of the considered opinion that, the accused has put forth a probable defense and the same has been proved on preponderance of probabilities and thereby has rebutted the legal presumptions which have worked in favour of the complainant.
21. Now, the onus shifts on the complainant to prove his case beyond all reasonable doubts.
Hence,
to prove his case beyond all reasonable doubts as per the provisions of section 145(1) of NI Act and also as per the verdict of the Hon'ble Apex Court, in the case of Indian Bank Association and others V/s Union of India and others, the sworn statement of the complainant has been treated as affidavit evidence.
Therefore, the self serving testimony of PW.1 is not sufficient material to believe the evidence of complainant as trust worthy and cogent.
opennyai_summary.arguments:
The Learned Defense Counsel vehemently argued that, when the financial capacity of the complainant is disputed, the initial burden is on the complainant to prove his case beyond all reasonable doubts, then only the legal presumptions under sections 118 and 139 of NI Act shall go in favour of the complainant.
The burden shifts on the accused to rebut the statutory presumption under section 118(a) & 139 of NI Act by raising probable defense and also proving the said probable defense by producing evidence on preponderance of probabilities.
Once, the accused establishes and proved his defense and thereby rebuts the legal presumptions, the onus shifts on the complainant to establish and prove his beyond all reasonable doubts.
